Wallace's essay, with its dateline and the manner of its sending, was consistent with Lyell and Hooker's statement that the two men had worked unknown to one another, and it was Wallace himself who had sent the essay to Darwin, with the express wish that Darwin forward it to Lyell if he thought it sufficiently novel and interesting.
同样，证据包没有说明华莱士在宣读之前是否知情、是否同意，这一点本文不作任何陈述。
Likewise, the evidence does not say whether Wallace knew of the reading beforehand or consented to it, and this article makes no statement either way.
The price is that it leaves no record of who did what.

whether Wallace knew of or consented to the reading beforehand is not recorded in the material and no statement is made;

W2-LINN.title: Darwin and Wallace, 'On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties…', Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society (1858), with the covering letter of Lyell and Hooker, Wikisource
W2-LINN.ref: en:On the tendency of species to form varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection

W2-PSM.title: 'Sketch of Alfred Russel Wallace', Popular Science Monthly, vol. 11 (June 1877), Wikisource
W2-PSM.ref: en:Popular Science Monthly/Volume 11/June 1877/Sketch of Alfred Russel Wallace

episode.outcome: The source closes the episode with Lyell and Hooker's reasons for presenting both men's material together, which Darwin had allowed. The heading records that the material was read on 1 July 1858. The letter itself proposes to read only extracts from Darwin's manuscript.
episode.quote: some of the leading results of his labours, as well as those of his able correspondent, should together be laid before the public

episode.outcome: The 1877 sketch says Wallace's paper was passed through Lyell to the Linnean Society and read on 1 July 1858 alongside Darwin's paper. It then turns to Wallace's later career: his return in 1862, his disagreement over human origins, his medals and his publications.
episode.quote: was read before that body on July 1, 1858, coincidently with the reading of Mr, Darwin's paper

additions.start: The first Part is devoted to
additions.end: from which we propose to read to the Society the extracts referred to
additions.why: The letter makes clear that only extracts ("a selection") from Darwin's manuscript were to be read to the Society, not the whole. Readers need this limit to understand what 'reading the material' meant on 1 July.

review.overall: The draft's statements about what the sources do and do not record hold against both full texts. The wording 'the evidence pack does not say' should become 'the sources do not record', and the piece should add the letter's claim that both authors 'unreservedly' handed over their papers and that only extracts were read. No fix-level misleading statement was found.
